/* First modification: TUrn on top or bottom */
@media only screen and (min-width:927px){ /*when viewport is larger than 927 turn on left, hide bottom logo*/
	.left {display:block !important;
		min-height:90px !important;}
	/*.right{float:right !important; margin: 0 0% 0 0%;} */
	.right {min-height:90px;}
	.bottom {display:none !important;}
	#navbar{width:100% !important;}
}
@media only screen and (max-width:938px){  /*when less than 867, turn on bottom */
	.left {display:none !important;}
	.right{float:none !important;     margin: 0 auto!important; min-height:55px; }
	.bottom {display:block !important;
		background-position-y:top !important;}

}




/*step 2: set proper logo for larger sizes */
@media only screen and (min-width:1170px){  /*larger than 1130---set .right size for large header */
	.left{background: url("https://www.openculture.com/wp-content/themes/openculture_v4a/images/open-culture-horizontal-logo-with-tagline.svg") no-repeat !important;
		  min-height:90px !important;}
	.right{width:740px ; margin: 0 2% 0 1%; text-align:right !important;}
}

@media only screen and (min-width:939px) and (max-width:1169px)  {  /*right ad, horizontal logo */
	.right{width:740px ; margin: 0 2% 0 1%; text-align:right !important;}
	.left{ background: url("https://www.openculture.com/wp-content/themes/openculture_v4a/images/open-culture-stacked-logo.svg") no-repeat !important;
			min-height:70px;
			background-position-x:center !important;
			}
	#clearfixheader{margin-top:.8rem !important;}
}

@media only screen and (min-width:814px) and (max-width:938px)  {  /* right ad, stacked logo */
	.right{width:740px ; margin: 0 2% 0 1% !important; text-align:right !important;}
	.left{ background: url("https://www.openculture.com/wp-content/themes/openculture_v4a/images/open-culture-stacked-logo.svg") no-repeat !important;
			min-height:70px;
			background-position-x:center !important;}
	#clearfixheader{margin-top:2.8rem !important;}
}


/* step 3 resize top ad */
/* sizes are: 728 x 90, 468x 60, 320x100 */

/*ads to right */
@media only screen and (max-width:813px) and (min-width:768px){  /* below 813, reduce right size for miniheader */
	.right{width:500px; text-align:center !important;}

}

}  /* cutoff for 728 AD at around 760 */

}

}

<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>There aren’t many ways to expe­ri­ence the ancient world. We can learn its lan­guages, at least the ones that have left behind deci­pher­able writ­ings; we can behold its arti­facts; we can vis­it its ruins. But noth­ing gets us quite as close to enter­ing the con­scious­ness of our dis­tant fore­bears as hear­ing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2nWf_OXdKz8">the new <em>Archae­ol­o­gist’s Note­book</em> video above</a>, Giselle Kirá­ly gives us a tour through ancient musi­cal his­to­ry, explain­ing the instru­ments of those times that sur­vive in one form or anoth­er today. That tour begins at a much ear­li­er point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punc­tu­at­ing their strug­gle for sur­vival with orga­nized sound.</p>
<p>As evi­dence, Kirá­ly points to the “tiny, exquis­ite­ly craft­ed flutes carved from ani­mal bone and mam­moth ivory” dis­cov­ered on cave floors around Europe. Sur­pris­ing­ly, when played in repli­ca form, these vul­ture- or swan-bone flutes actu­al­ly sound some­what Mid­dle East­ern. But what­ev­er the styl­is­tic traits of the music their orig­i­nal play­ers pro­duced, that music had the poten­tial to con­fer ben­e­fits beyond imme­di­ate plea­sure: “It would’ve con­nect­ed peo­ple, built cohe­sion with­in the com­mu­ni­ty,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the liv­ing with some spir­i­tu­al world.” Each of the oth­er dis­cov­ered or recon­struct­ed instru­ments, like swingable “bull­roar­ers,” bone rasps, and litho­phones (of the kind <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2019/09/watch-an-archaeologist-play-the-lithophone.html">pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture</a>) would have played its own son­ic part to that end.</p>
<p>Kirá­ly also dis­cuss­es the lav­ish­ly dec­o­rat­ed Lyres of Ur, the world’s old­est sur­viv­ing stringed instru­ments; a 3,500-year-old Egypt­ian long-necked lute with a gui­tar-like fin­ger­board; and a set of 65 Chi­nese <em>bianzhong </em>bells cov­er­ing a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also impor­tant are the means of record­ing it, an ancient exam­ple of which Kirá­ly cites in the <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2023/03/hear-the-oldest-song-in-the-world-a-sumerian-hymn-written-3400-years-ago.html">Hur­ri­an Hymn to Nikkal</a> inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the old­est known com­plete musi­cal nota­tion. Cen­turies lat­er, in the Greek-speak­ing world — and in the more mon­u­men­tal form of a mar­ble stele — a man named Seik­i­los record­ed an epi­taph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2015/05/hear-the-seikilos-epitaph-the-oldest-complete-song-in-the-world.html">old­est com­plete­ly pre­served, ful­ly playable musi­cal com­po­si­tion</a> exhort the lis­ten­er: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients need­ed to hear this no less, per­haps, than we do.</p>

      			<p><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-1129048 native-lazyload-js-fallback" src="https://www.openculture.com/wp-content/plugins/native-lazyload/assets/images/placeholder.svg" alt width="1419" height="1109" data-src="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box.png" data-srcset="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box.png 1419w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-360x281.png 360w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-1024x800.png 1024w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-240x188.png 240w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-768x600.png 768w" data-sizes="auto, (max-width: 1419px) 100vw, 1419px"><noscript><img loading="lazy" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-1129048" src="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box.png" alt width="1419" height="1109" srcset="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box.png 1419w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-360x281.png 360w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-1024x800.png 1024w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-240x188.png 240w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/25221615/Retro-Swanson-Turkey-Dinner-Box-768x600.png 768w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1419px) 100vw, 1419px"></noscript></p>
<p>“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sen­sa­tion of eat­ing and drink­ing — is a strange and com­plex and com­pli­cat­ed thing,” <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1976/11/22/archives/westchester-weekly-what-taste-means-to-one-man-in-the-kitchen.html?eafs_enabled=false">writes New York <em>Times</em> food edi­tor Craig Clai­borne</a>. “I am con­vinced that there are a mul­ti­tude of peo­ple (Amer­i­cans, most­ly, to judge by the peo­ple who buy TV din­ners and frozen piz­zas) who have no taste what­so­ev­er.” That col­umn was pub­lished almost exact­ly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such con­ve­nience-ori­ent­ed food prod­ucts had already enjoyed promi­nence in Amer­i­can life for two decades. Though it could hard­ly have made a dent in the pop­u­lar­i­ty of TV din­ners, Clai­borne’s typ­i­cal­ly waspish aside did draw a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1977/01/12/archives/westchester-weekly-letters.html">let­ter of objec­tion</a> from one Ros­alie Levine of Lake­wood, Cal­i­for­nia.</p>
<p>“I live alone, I must con­trol my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV din­ner’s price “can­not pos­si­bly be bet­tered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready din­ner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to pre­pare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up after­ward.” While none of these advan­tages were acci­den­tal, the oft-told sto­ry of the con­cep­t’s emer­gence begins with a cor­po­rate cri­sis.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>“In 1953, some­one at Swan­son colos­sal­ly mis­cal­cu­lat­ed the lev­el of the Amer­i­can appetite for Thanks­giv­ing turkey, leav­ing the com­pa­ny with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/tray-bon-96872641/">as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it</a>. “Inspired by the trays of pre-pre­pared food served on air­lines,” Swan­son sales­man Ger­ry Thomas set the machin­ery in motion to pack­age the unwant­ed meat with gravy and sides like corn­bread and sweet pota­toes, ready for stock­ing in Amer­i­ca’s frozen-food aisles.</p>
<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/Hy-M7oieUNo?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>The fol­low­ing year, Swan­son sold ten mil­lion such “TV din­ners,” a name attrib­uted to both the shape of the box­es and the form of enter­tain­ment fam­i­lies tend­ed to enjoy while eat­ing the meals with­in. “In 1950, only 9 per­cent of U.S. house­holds had tele­vi­sion sets — but by 1955, the num­ber had risen to more than 64 per­cent, and by 1960, to more than 87 per­cent,” writes Kovie Biako­lo in <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/brief-history-tv-dinner-180976039/">a more recent Smith­son­ian piece</a>. (Among the Smith­son­ian Insti­tu­tion’s hold­ings, inci­den­tal­ly, is <a href="https://www.si.edu/object/swanson-tv-dinner-tray%3Anmah_741033">an orig­i­nal Swan­son TV din­ner tray</a>.) Anoth­er break­through came with the intro­duc­tion of microwave-safe trays, bring­ing total prepa­ra­tion time under ten min­utes. Dur­ing the COVID-19 pan­dem­ic, Amer­i­cans rekin­dled their love affair with frozen meals, “spend­ing near­ly 50 per­cent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”</p>
<p>Where hol­i­day and com­mer­cial lore inter­sect, the details tend to get com­pli­cat­ed. Swan­son’s TV din­ner did have its prece­dents: the core tech­nol­o­gy for quick-freez­ing pack­aged foods was invent­ed over a cen­tu­ry ago by entre­pre­neur Clarence Bird­s­eye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remem­bers as “lit­tle cryo­genic mir­a­cles”), and in the late 1940s, dif­fer­ent com­pa­nies planned or attempt­ed to bring frozen meals to mar­ket under brands like Stra­to-Plates, FridgiDin­ners, and One-Eyed Eski­mo. None of those names tapped into the tech­nol­o­gy trans­form­ing not just Amer­i­can mass cul­ture, but also the Amer­i­can way of life. In the fifties, asso­ci­a­tions with tele­vi­sion (and, indeed, with air trav­el) car­ried a kind of sophis­ti­ca­tion they cer­tain­ly don’t have today. Per­haps Craig Clai­borne would be pleased that Amer­i­cans nev­er quite accept­ed microwaved TV din­ners as a sub­sti­tute for the Thanks­giv­ing meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is anoth­er mat­ter entire­ly.</p>

<p>Alice’s Restau­rant. It’s now a Thanks­giv­ing clas­sic, and some­thing of a tra­di­tion around here. Record­ed in 1967, the 18+ minute coun­ter­cul­ture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, start­ing on Thanks­giv­ing Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hip­pie-bat­ing police offi­cer, by the name of <a href="http://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/14/obituaries/william-j-obanhein-alice-s-restaurant-lawman-69.html">William “Obie” Oban­hein</a>, arrest­ed Arlo for lit­ter­ing. (Cul­tur­al foot­note: Obie pre­vi­ous­ly posed for sev­er­al Nor­man Rock­well paint­ings, includ­ing the well-known paint­ing, <a href="http://www.artchive.com/artchive/r/rockwell/rockwell_runaway.jpg">“The Run­away,”</a> that graced a <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20180723115710/https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2012/05/08/archives/a-fond-farewell-to-an-iconic-policeman.html">1958 cov­er of </a><em><a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20180723115710/https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2012/05/08/archives/a-fond-farewell-to-an-iconic-policeman.html">The Sat­ur­day Evening Post</a></em>.) In fair­ly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a mis­de­meanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the sto­ry isn’t over. Not by a long shot.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Lat­er, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the pet­ty crime iron­i­cal­ly becomes a basis for dis­qual­i­fy­ing him from mil­i­tary ser­vice in the Viet­nam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bit­ter­ness as the song builds into a satir­i­cal protest against the war: “I’m sit­tin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, hous­es and vil­lages after bein’ a lit­ter­bug.” And then we’re back to the cheery cho­rus again: “You can get any­thing you want, at Alice’s Restau­rant.”</p>
<p>We have fea­tured Guthrie’s clas­sic dur­ing past years. But, for this Thanks­giv­ing, we give you the illus­trat­ed ver­sion.</p>

      			<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/I0rkpF49Deo?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve often fea­tured the charm­ing and infor­ma­tive posters of <em><a href="https://www.youtube.com/@DomainofScience">Domain of Sci­ence</a></em>. Each one maps out a dif­fer­ent field of knowl­edge: there’s <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2017/12/the-map-of-biology-animation-shows-how-all-the-different-fields-in-biology-fit-together.html">biol­o­gy</a>, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2026/06/the-map-of-physics-animation.html">physics</a>, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2017/05/the-map-of-chemistry-new-animation-summarizes-the-entire-field-of-chemistry-in-12-minutes.html">chem­istry</a>, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2020/08/the-map-of-quantum-physics-a-colorful-animation-explains-the-often-misunderstood-branch-of-science.html">quan­tum physics</a>, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2022/05/the-animated-map-of-quantum-computing-a-visual-introduction-to-the-future-of-computing.html">quan­tum com­put­ing</a>, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/?p=1124762">fun­gi</a>, and many oth­ers besides. But with his lat­est map, <em>Domain of Sci­ence</em> cre­ator Dominic Wal­li­man has turned away from the sci­en­tif­ic realm — or rather, he’s ven­tured into the larg­er intel­lec­tu­al ter­ri­to­ry out of which it emerged. His new <a href="https://domainofscience.com/the-map-of-philosophy">Map of Phi­los­o­phy</a>, which he explains in <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I0rkpF49Deo">the video above</a>, includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiq­ui­ty like Thales, Laozi, Con­fu­cius, and the Bud­dha, who lived and died before sci­ence as we know it.</p>
<p>That hard­ly means that they’ve become irrel­e­vant today. There still exist soci­eties described as Con­fu­cian or Bud­dhist, of course, but in the West­ern world, we’re more like­ly to refer back to — and, in many cas­es, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Pla­to, and Aris­to­tle. “They basi­cal­ly laid the intel­lec­tu­al foun­da­tion of West­ern phi­los­o­phy, sci­ence, and polit­i­cal thought,” says Wal­li­man. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unex­am­ined life is not worth liv­ing, which “hits pret­ty hard in the age of the dis­trac­tion econ­o­my.”)</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Though often men­tioned togeth­er, these three ancient Greeks occu­py slight­ly dif­fer­ent posi­tions on the philo­soph­i­cal map, with Socrates clos­er to the land of ethics, Pla­to to meta­physics, and Aris­to­tle to epis­te­mol­o­gy.</p>
<p>As Wal­li­man explains, “epis­te­mol­o­gy stud­ies knowl­edge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it dif­fers from faith or opin­ions,” while also seek­ing out its lim­its. Aris­totle’s rig­or in test­ing and orga­niz­ing knowl­edge makes him, in a sense, one of the ear­li­est sci­en­tists. Though his body of the­o­ry may no longer be our best means of under­stand­ing how the world works, his sys­tem­at­ic pur­suit of such an under­stand­ing set him apart from much of the ancient intel­lec­tu­al world. The islands off the coast of the map’s main­land rep­re­sent sub­fields still active­ly explored today, like the philoso­phies of mind, lan­guage, pol­i­tics, reli­gion, and sci­ence — which, for all its pres­tige, remains as sub­ject to philo­soph­i­cal inquiry as any oth­er area of human endeav­or. The map of phi­los­o­phy shows us not a rar­efied, most­ly aban­doned ter­ri­to­ry, but the place where we all live our lives, exam­ined or oth­er­wise.</p>

      			<div class="oc-video-container"><iframe loading="lazy" frameborder="0" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/videoseries?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg" width="560"></iframe></div>
<p>Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and sev­er­al adap­ta­tions of <a href="https://www.eapoe.org/works/tales/usherf.htm">“The Fall of the House of Ush­er”</a> will almost cer­tain­ly come near the top. At first glance, that sto­ry of a man pay­ing a vis­it to an old friend who lives with his twin sis­ter in their fam­i­ly’s grand house — each of the lat­ter three well advanced into a dif­fer­ent process of dete­ri­o­ra­tion — might seem too short, as well as too light on con­flict to trans­late into a con­ven­tion­al screen­play. Yet it’s also full of cin­e­mat­i­cal­ly irre­sistible images, from the some­how ruinous yet whol­ly intact tit­u­lar man­sion to the blood­i­ly wretched sis­ter throw­ing her­self upon the ter­ri­fied broth­er who entombed her alive while their ances­tral home col­laps­es around them.</p>
<p>Of the twen­ty or thir­ty ver­sions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” so far made for the screen, the most cel­e­brat­ed remains the one Jean Epstein direct­ed in 1928. <a href="https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher-1928">Offi­cial­ly des­ig­nat­ing it as one of the “great movies,”</a> Roger Ebert calls that pic­ture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunt­ing spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast mar­ble expanse, inter­rupt­ed here and there by an item of fur­ni­ture that seems dwarfed by the sur­round­ing empti­ness. An odd stair­case ris­es from one dis­tant cor­ner. It is not impos­si­ble that this vision, in one of the best-known French sur­re­al­ist films, inspired the design­ers of the great hall of Xanadu in <em>Cit­i­zen Kane</em>.”</p>
<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/hD8uQzu0IL0?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>The avant-garde film­mak­ing duo James Sib­ley Wat­son Jr. and Melville Web­ber (in col­lab­o­ra­tion with e. e. cum­mings, who con­tributed to the script) could hard­ly man­age the same scale of pro­duc­tion design for <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eh1Fnxctjsw">their own short adap­ta­tion of Poe’s sto­ry</a>, which hap­pened to come out the same year.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>But the result­ing Expres­sion­ist take on the mate­r­i­al has also been high­ly acclaimed, and through <a href="https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg">this YouTube playlist of Poe films</a>, you can expe­ri­ence not just both of them, but also oth­er adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” by <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4f3ZxoLTHkk">idio­syn­crat­ic Czech ani­ma­tor Jan Švankma­jer</a> and <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EgktFwcVXCY">B‑movie pow­er­house Roger Cor­man</a>. Sen­si­tive to Poe’s sen­sa­tion­al­ist appeal and air of trans­gres­sive deca­dence, Cor­man end­ed up direct­ing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” near­ly all of which star Vin­cent Price.</p>
<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/ZzyYzK94UU4?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>It’s fair to say that no film actor is more close­ly asso­ci­at­ed with Poe than Price, a link Tim Bur­ton <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hD8uQzu0IL0">cel­e­brat­ed in ani­ma­tion</a> at the begin­ning of his career. Price even played the writer him­self in <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZzyYzK94UU4&list=PLGECP2JNbcRg&index=7"><em>An Evening with Edgar Allan</em> <em>Poe</em></a>, a spe­cial from 1970 in which he recites  “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” “The Pit and the Pen­du­lum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapt­ed Poe sto­ry of them all, also appears on <a href="https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg">the playlist</a> in var­i­ous forms: an <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=avB4bs4Q6DU">ear­ly D. W. Grif­fith fea­ture</a>, the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RW6fdqnN0E0">direc­to­r­i­al debut of Jules Dassin</a>, an <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WAXB2H3SsFg">ani­mat­ed short nar­rat­ed by James Mason</a>, a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pXMZeSZS_-A">British psy­cho­log­i­cal thriller</a>, and a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yWworPqU668">trans­po­si­tion into mod­ern-day New Orleans</a>. And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watch­ing through all 25 of these films, con­sid­er watch­ing the recent, well-received <em>Fall of the House of Ush­er </em>minis­eries on Net­flix — an enter­tain­ment plat­form that sat­is­fies much the same appetites Poe’s sto­ries have been feed­ing for near­ly two cen­turies.</p>

      			<p><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignleft wp-image-1065619 size-full native-lazyload-js-fallback" src="https://www.openculture.com/wp-content/plugins/native-lazyload/assets/images/placeholder.svg" alt width="900" height="1144" data-src="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2019/06/03224901/Marie_Curie_Nobel-Chem-e1559627357864.jpg"><noscript><img loading="lazy" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignleft wp-image-1065619 size-full" src="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2019/06/03224901/Marie_Curie_Nobel-Chem-e1559627357864.jpg" alt width="900" height="1144"></noscript><br>
For most of sci­en­tif­ic his­to­ry, women who made con­tri­bu­tions to var­i­ous fields have been side­lined or ignored in favor of male col­leagues, who reaped fame, pro­fes­sion­al recog­ni­tion, and cash rewards that come with pres­ti­gious prizes like the Nobel. Cor­nell his­to­ri­an of sci­ence <a href="https://sts.cornell.edu/margaret-rossiter">Mar­garet Rossiter</a> coined<a href="https://www.openculture.com/2025/12/matilda-effect.html"> the term “The Matil­da Effect”</a> to describe sex­ist bias in the sci­ences. Rossiter’s work and pop­u­lar reap­praisals like book-turned-film <em><a href="https://amzn.to/2HTG1jS">Hid­den Fig­ures</a> </em>have inspired oth­er women in acad­e­mia to search for for­got­ten female sci­en­tists, and to find them, lit­er­al­ly, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2019/02/womens-hidden-contributions-to-modern-science-get-revealed-by-new-study.html">in foot­notes</a>.</p>
<p>When sys­tem­at­ic dis­crim­i­na­tion lim­its oppor­tu­ni­ties for any group, those who do receive recog­ni­tion, the excep­tions to the rule, must often be tru­ly excep­tion­al to suc­ceed. There has been lit­tle doubt, both in her life­time and in the many decades after­ward, that Marie Curie was such a per­son. Although forced to study sci­ence in secret at a clan­des­tine “<a href="https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html">Float­ing Uni­ver­si­ty</a>” in her native Poland—since the uni­ver­si­ties refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodows­ka in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was award­ed not one, but two Nobel Prizes.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Curie and her hus­band Pierre shared the<a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/"> Nobel Prize</a> <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/">in Physics</a> with Antoine Hen­ri Bec­quer­el, dis­cov­er­er of radioac­tiv­i­ty, in 1903. The sec­ond prize, in Chem­istry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recog­ni­tion of her ser­vices to the advance­ment of chem­istry by the dis­cov­ery of the ele­ments radi­um and polo­ni­um, by the iso­la­tion of radi­um and the study of the nature and com­pounds of this remark­able ele­ment.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first per­son to win twice, and the only per­son to win in two dif­fer­ent sci­ences.</p>
<p>These are but a hand­ful of achieve­ments in a string of firsts for Curie: denied posi­tions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, award­ed the degree in 1903 by the <a href="https://www.sorbonne-universite.fr/en/university/history-and-heritage/history">Sor­bonne</a>, the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her exam­in­ers,” notes the site <a href="https://www.famousscientists.org/marie-curie/">Famous Sci­en­tists</a>, “were of the view that she had made the great­est con­tri­bu­tion to sci­ence ever found in a Ph.D. the­sis.” Three years lat­er, after Pierre was killed in an acci­dent, Marie was offered his pro­fes­sor­ship and became the first female pro­fes­sor at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Paris.</p>
<p>Curie suc­ceed­ed not in the absence of, but in spite of the sex­ist obsta­cles placed in her path at near­ly every stage in her career. After she received her doc­tor­ate, the Curies were invit­ed to the Roy­al Insti­tu­tion in Lon­don. Only Pierre was per­mit­ted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Com­mit­tee decid­ed to hon­or only her hus­band and Bec­quer­el. The Acad­e­my relent­ed when Pierre protest­ed. Curie fell vic­tim to a wave of xeno­pho­bia and anti-Semi­tism (though she was not Jew­ish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famous­ly in the so-called “Drey­fus Affair.”</p>
<p>In 1911, the year of her sec­ond Nobel, Curie was passed over for mem­ber­ship in the <a href="https://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/">French Acad­e­my of Sci­ences</a>. It would take anoth­er 51 years before the first woman, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Perey">Mar­guerite Perey,</a> a for­mer doc­tor­al stu­dent of Curie, would be elect­ed to that body. That same year, Curie was per­se­cut­ed relent­less­ly by the French press, the pub­lic, and her sci­en­tif­ic rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physi­cist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s for­mer stu­dents.</p>
<p>But no mat­ter how many men in posi­tions of pow­er want­ed to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2017/12/read-the-dont-let-the-bastards-get-you-down-letter-that-albert-einstein-sent-to-marie-curie-during-a-time-of-personal-crisis-1911.html">influ­en­tial sci­en­tists</a> and politi­cians who rec­og­nized the supreme val­ue of her work and the need to help her con­tin­ue it. After her sec­ond Nobel Prize, her native coun­try final­ly rec­og­nized her with the offer to direct her own lab­o­ra­to­ry in War­saw. Curie turned it down to focus on direct­ing the Curie Lab­o­ra­to­ry in the Radi­um Insti­tute of the Uni­ver­si­ty of Paris, which she found­ed in 1914, a major achieve­ment and, again, only a small part of her lega­cy.</p>
<p>Curie is known, of course, fore­most for her excep­tion­al sci­en­tif­ic work, but also for open­ing doors for women in sci­ence all over the world, though much of that door-open­ing may only have hap­pened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t hap­pened at all yet. Inci­den­tal­ly, in the fol­low­ing year, the Curies’ daugh­ter Irène Joliot-Curie and her hus­band Frédéric Joliot-Curie were joint­ly award­ed the Nobel Prize in Chem­istry. Since then, only sev­en oth­er women have claimed that hon­or, and <a href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-the-nobel-prizes-missing-female-scientists/?redirect=1">only five women, includ­ing Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics</a>, out of 230 win­ners total.</p>
<p>There may be noth­ing yet like gen­der par­i­ty in the sci­ences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women sci­en­tists run­ning women-owned com­pa­nies, women-found­ed research insti­tutes and aca­d­e­m­ic depart­ments, and, like the famous Curies, mak­ing <a href="https://www.thoughtco.com/famous-women-in-chemistry-609453">major con­tri­bu­tions to chem­istry</a>. Per­haps not long from now, many of those excep­tion­al sci­en­tists will be as well-known and wide­ly cel­e­brat­ed as Marie Curie.</p>
<p>Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.</p>

      			<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/4APkXceabVY?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>These days, if you want to see a par­tic­u­lar paint­ing, you can almost cer­tain­ly pull it up online in sec­onds. In more and more cas­es, the res­o­lu­tion of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a lev­el of detail is unavail­able in a muse­um, of course, but also dif­fi­cult to access even if you owned the phys­i­cal art­work in ques­tion. Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured such lux­u­ri­ant­ly dig­i­tized paint­ings as <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2020/05/the-largest-most-detailed-photograph-of-rembrandts-the-night-watch-is-now-online-zoom-in-see-every-brush-stroke.html"><em>The Night Watch</em></a>, <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2021/07/a-gallery-of-1800-super-high-resolution-images-of-classic-paintings.html"><em>Girl with a Pearl Ear­ring</em></a>, and <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2022/03/a-digital-archive-of-hieronymus-boschs-complete-works.html"><em>The Gar­den of Earth­ly Delights</em></a>. But there’s at least one cel­e­brat­ed work of Dutch mas­ters whose view­ing expe­ri­ence can nev­er tru­ly be repli­cat­ed on the inter­net: the <em>Ghent Altar­piece</em>, also called the <em>Ado­ra­tion of the Mys­tic Lamb</em>, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.</p>
<p>After watch­ing <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4APkXceabVY">the video from <em>The Gaze</em></a> above, you’ll sure­ly want to take as close as pos­si­ble a look at <a href="https://closertovaneyck.kikirpa.be/ghentaltarpiece/#home">the online <em>Ghent Altar­piece</em></a>, seek­ing out such high­light­ed details as the indi­vid­ual hairs on Adam’s beard, the real­is­ti­cal­ly awk­ward expres­sions on the faces of the angel cho­rus, and the iden­ti­fi­able cru­ci­fix­ion scene pinned to a pil­grim’s hat.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>But that may only stoke your desire to make a pil­grim­age of your own, to Bel­gium, where you can see the real thing care­ful­ly placed in St. Bavo’s Cathe­dral. In the ear­ly fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, when that insti­tu­tion was called St. John the Bap­tist’s Church, its war­den was the wealthy mer­chant Jodocus Vijd. Hav­ing endowed a new chapel, Vijd also com­mis­sioned the van Eyck broth­ers to cre­ate an altar­piece spec­tac­u­lar enough to secure him a spot in the after­life. The result was one of the ear­li­est mas­ter­pieces of oil paint­ing.</p>
<p>Even apart from that des­ig­na­tion (to say noth­ing of its being <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2020/12/how-jan-van-eycks-masterpiece-the-ghent-altarpiece-became-the-most-stolen-work-of-art-in-history.html">the most stolen work of art in his­to­ry</a>), it has enjoyed an impres­sive after­life of its own. Of the many who have trav­eled to behold it <em>in situ</em> at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecsta­sy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But oth­ers have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it before­hand, by all the atten­tion the artists put into inte­grat­ing the work with its sur­round­ings. The light with­in its images, for exam­ple, is paint­ed in such a way as to match the light stream­ing into the cathe­dral itself. Those who look close­ly at the gem worn by the fore­most singing angel will see a reflec­tion of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the know­ing gaze of the sac­ri­fi­cial lamb, they’re all but guar­an­teed to have a reli­gious expe­ri­ence — though whether its nature is Chris­t­ian, artis­tic, or oth­er­wise will depend, as it does with all endur­ing art, on the indi­vid­ual view­er.</p>

      			<p><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-1129023 native-lazyload-js-fallback" src="https://www.openculture.com/wp-content/plugins/native-lazyload/assets/images/placeholder.svg" alt width="720" height="456" data-src="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1.jpg" data-srcset="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1.jpg 720w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1-360x228.jpg 360w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1-240x152.jpg 240w" data-sizes="auto, (max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px"><noscript><img loading="lazy" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-1129023" src="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1.jpg" alt width="720" height="456" srcset="https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1.jpg 720w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1-360x228.jpg 360w, https://cdn8.openculture.com/2026/11/22225235/isaac-newton-list-of-sins-1-240x152.jpg 240w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px"></noscript></p>
<p>The Aris­totelian notion of “man” as a “ratio­nal ani­mal” has seen its share of detrac­tors, from the Cyn­ics to Bertrand Rus­sell to near­ly the whole of Post­struc­tural­ist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to com­press the debate between intel­lect and pas­sion into a pithy apho­rism: “Man is a ratio­nal ani­mal who always los­es his tem­per when he is called upon to act in accor­dance with the dic­tates of rea­son.”</p>
<p>We no longer need clever ver­bal barbs to refute too-opti­mistic assess­ments of human behav­ior. Eco­nom­ics is catch­ing up: we have the lan­guage of neu­ro­science and psy­chol­o­gy, which con­sis­tent­ly tells us that humans decid­ed­ly do <em>not</em> behave ratio­nal­ly very often, but are <a href="http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352154615000881">dri­ven by bias and biol­o­gy in inex­plic­a­ble ways</a>. And for over a hun­dred years now, we’ve known that the clock­work New­ton­ian view of the phys­i­cal uni­verse turns out to be a much messier and inde­ter­mi­nate affair, as does the uni­verse of the human mind.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Why, then, has so much eco­nom­ic the­o­ry oper­at­ed with a kind of dogged Aris­totelian­ism, insist­ing that the units of cap­i­tal­ist soci­ety, the work­ers, man­agers, investors, con­sumers, own­ers, renters, spec­u­la­tors, etc. behave in pre­dictable ways? We have case after case show­ing that intel­li­gence and crit­i­cal rea­son­ing often have lit­tle to do with suc­cess or fail­ure in the mar­ket. In such cas­es, how­ev­er, one often hears the “mad­ness of crowds” or oth­er clichés invoked as an expla­na­tion.</p>
<p>To illus­trate, mar­ket reporters and busi­ness writ­ers have seized upon the sto­ry of Isaac Newton’s spec­tac­u­lar rise and fall in the so-called “<a href="https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofEngland/South-Sea-Bubble/">South Sea Bub­ble</a>” of 1720. We find the sto­ry in Ben­jamin Graham’s 1949 clas­sic <a href="https://link.amazon/B09D6TAhV"><em>The Intel­li­gent Investor</em></a>, a wide­ly-read book that attrib­ut­es the irra­tional­i­ty of mar­ket sys­tems to an anthro­po­mor­phic enti­ty named “Mr. Mar­ket.”</p>
<p>Gra­ham writes,</p>
<blockquote><p><em>Back in the spring of 1720, Sir Isaac New­ton owned shares in the South Sea Com­pa­ny, the hottest stock in Eng­land. Sens­ing that the mar­ket was get­ting out of hand, the great physi­cist mut­tered that he ‘<strong>could cal­cu­late the motions of the heav­en­ly bod­ies, but not the mad­ness of the peo­ple</strong>.’ New­ton dumped his South Sea shares, pock­et­ing a 100% prof­it total­ing £7,000. But just months lat­er, swept up in the wild enthu­si­asm of the mar­ket, New­ton jumped back in at a much high­er price — and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 mil­lion in [2002–2003’s] mon­ey. For the rest of his life, he for­bade any­one to speak the words ‘South Sea’ in his pres­ence.</em></p></blockquote>
<p>The quo­ta­tion in bold may or may not have been uttered by New­ton, but the events Gra­ham describes did indeed hap­pen. As the <a href="https://jasonzweig.com/isaac-newton-learned-about-financial-gravity-the-hard-way/"><em>Wall Street Jour­nal</em>’s Jason Zweig relates</a>, Uni­ver­si­ty of Min­neso­ta pro­fes­sor <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Odlyzko">Andrew Odlyzko</a> found that “New­ton had shift­ed from a pru­dent investor with his mon­ey spread across sev­er­al secu­ri­ties to a spec­u­la­tor who had plunged essen­tial­ly all of his cap­i­tal into a sin­gle stock. The great sci­en­tist was chas­ing hot per­for­mance as des­per­ate­ly as a day trad­er in 1999 or many bit­coin buy­ers in 2017.” (Odlyzko esti­mates New­ton’s loss­es at clos­er to $4 mil­lion.) Per­haps it was not a metaphor­i­cal “Mr. Mar­ket” who cost New­ton up to 77% “on his worst pur­chas­es,” nor was it wide­spread “wild enthusiasm”—the mass move­ment of pas­sion that Enlight­en­ment philoso­phers so feared.</p>
<p>Per­haps it was New­ton him­self who, <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20181229001933/http://www.businessinsider.com/isaac-newton-lost-a-fortune-on-englands-hottest-stock-2016-1">Ele­na Holod­ny writes at <em>Busi­ness Insid­er</em></a><em>,</em> “let his emo­tions get the best of him, and got swayed by the irra­tional­i­ty of the crowd.” Maybe it’s more accu­rate to say New­ton suc­cumbed to greed when the bub­ble expand­ed. “Through­out his­to­ry,” <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20160830223425/https://www.marketwatch.com/story/investor-lessons-from-a-market-bubble-that-cost-isaac-newton-a-bundle-2016-08-25">Bar­bara Kollmey­er writes at <em>Mar­ket Watch</em></a> in her inter­view with <a href="https://link.amazon/B04Ef22zp">author Richard Dale</a>, “people—especially those at the top rung of society—have been greedy and gullible par­tic­i­pants in finan­cial bub­bles. And Sir Isaac New­ton was only human, after all.” (How many at the top rung of soci­ety fell prey to Bernie Madoff’s schemes? And a cen­tu­ry before the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sea_Company">South Sea Bub­ble</a>, hun­dreds of wealthy investors lost their shirts in the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania">Dutch Tulip Bulb craze.</a>)</p>
<p>Some busi­ness writ­ers, like invest­ment edi­tor <a href="http://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/personalfinance/investing/10848995/How-not-to-invest-like-Sir-Isaac-Newton.html">Richard Evans at <em>The Tele­graph,</em></a> rec­om­mend a cal­cu­la­ble for­mu­la to avoid los­ing a for­tune in bub­bles, advice that takes ratio­nal agency for grant­ed. Per­haps it should not. In addi­tion to cit­ing the con­ta­gion of crowds, near­ly every dis­cus­sion of Newton’s fol­ly allows that a fail­ure of emo­tion­al dis­ci­pline played a sig­nif­i­cant role. Ben­jamin Gra­ham invokes anoth­er Aris­totelian notion—the idea that “char­ac­ter” counts as much or more than intel­li­gence when it comes to invest­ing. “The investor’s chief prob­lem,” he writes, “and even his worst enemy—is like­ly to be him­self.”</p>
<p>Far few­er com­menters note that the South Sea ven­ture was itself a fail­ure of char­ac­ter from its incep­tion. The com­pa­ny had secured an exclu­sive monop­oly on trade with South Amer­i­ca; much of that trade involved sell­ing slaves. It is also the case that the com­pa­ny arti­fi­cial­ly inflat­ed its stock prices, and col­lud­ed with sev­er­al MPs in insid­er trad­ing schemes. The so-called <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble_Act">“Bub­ble Act” of Par­lia­ment in 1720</a>, pre­sum­ably passed to pre­vent crash­es like the one that dev­as­tat­ed New­ton, turned out to be a cor­po­rate give­away. The terms of the act had been dic­tat­ed by the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sea_Company">South Sea Com­pa­ny</a> in order to pre­vent oth­er com­pa­nies from poach­ing their investors. Although these cir­cum­stances are well-known to eco­nom­ic his­to­ri­ans, they rarely make their way into com­men­tary on Newton’s great loss.</p>
<p>Econ­o­mists instead tend to blame abstrac­tions for eco­nom­ic events like the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sea_Company">South Sea Bub­ble</a>, or they blame the over­reach­ing prof­it-seek­ing of investors, and maybe for good rea­son. The oth­er expla­na­tions haunt the mar­gins: the inher­ent­ly exploita­tive nature of most forms of cor­po­rate cap­i­tal­ism, and the cor­rup­tion and col­lu­sion between the state and pri­vate enter­prise that inhibits fair com­pe­ti­tion and makes it impos­si­ble for investors to eval­u­ate the sit­u­a­tion trans­par­ent­ly. For all of his sci­en­tif­ic and math­e­mat­i­cal genius, Isaac New­ton was no exception—he was just as sub­ject to irra­tional greed as the next investor, and to the preda­to­ry machi­na­tions of “mar­ket forces.”</p>

<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/-bqA022KHvs?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>

<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>Most of us remem­ber where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learn­ing that the most famous of all French cathe­drals had been bad­ly dam­aged rather than com­plete­ly destroyed, it still felt as if some­thing irre­place­able had been lost. It made no dif­fer­ence whether we’d actu­al­ly been to the place, as I had­n’t at the time. When I did final­ly make it to Paris four years lat­er, Notre-Dame’s restora­tion was still under­way, and con­struc­tion walls pre­vent­ed any­one from see­ing much of any­thing at ground lev­el, let alone enter­ing. Yet crowds still gath­ered to take pic­tures in the square out­side, appar­ent­ly find­ing that prox­im­i­ty to such a civ­i­liza­tion­al land­mark was enough, even in its par­tial­ly ruined and inac­ces­si­ble state.</p>
<p>Even with­out a chance to step inside, expe­ri­enc­ing Notre-Dame’s sur­round­ings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban con­text of Paris, cer­tain­ly deep­ens one’s under­stand­ing of the beau­ty of the cathe­dral itself. So does vis­it­ing oth­er, less wide­ly known exam­ples of the form, as shown by archi­tec­ture-and-his­to­ry YouTu­ber Manuel Bra­vo in <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-bqA022KHvs">his new video above</a>.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Ordi­nary tourists in Paris may make a bee­line for Notre-Dame, but they’re hard­ly like­ly to find their way out to the oth­er medieval cathe­drals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glo­ri­ous in their own way, they’re per­haps even more valu­able in pro­vid­ing the con­text of Goth­ic church archi­tec­ture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.</p>
<p>As Bra­vo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade rep­re­sents “the moment in which Goth­ic façade achieves its most bal­anced syn­the­sis. The exper­i­ments and inno­va­tions of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, dis­ci­plined, and uni­fied into a com­po­si­tion in which no ele­ment appears arbi­trary or inde­pen­dent from the whole.” Among its most influ­en­tial appre­ci­a­tors was Vic­tor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Goth­ic archi­tec­ture was being demol­ished. His roman­tic evo­ca­tions of the medieval built envi­ron­ment in <em>Notre-Dame de Paris</em> (in Eng­lish, <a href="https://link.amazon/B09LwxgEJ"><em>The Hunch­back of Notre-Dame</em></a>) helped save the much dete­ri­o­rat­ed tit­u­lar struc­ture, which received an ambi­tious ren­o­va­tion under <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Viollet-le-Duc">Eugène Vio­l­let-le-Duc</a> between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond peri­od accu­ra­cy, adding such non-orig­i­nal details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain vis­i­ble dur­ing the lat­est restora­tion work. Vis­i­tors today may notice that the inte­ri­or does­n’t look exact­ly like it used to, but some will appre­ci­ate that even a mon­u­ment like Notre-Dame must change with the cen­turies.</p>

			<div id="post-1128994" class="post-1128994 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-history category-technology">
      			<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/F20zQmyZa20?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>“It’s a sun­ny morn­ing in ancient Greece. Stu­dents have start­ed gath­er­ing in the Acad­e­my, but their famous teacher Pla­to is nowhere to be seen.” The great philoso­pher has, it seems, “over­slept and missed his own lec­ture.” The sun and the sound of ear­ly-ris­ing ani­mals may have failed Pla­to that day, as the sto­ry goes, but nev­er would he let it hap­pen again — at least after he got the mech­a­nism worked out for the first alarm clock in his­to­ry. Its design involves a series of con­tain­ers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accu­mu­lates in the penul­ti­mate, sealed ves­sel, air is pushed out through the flute embed­ded in its wall, pro­duc­ing some­thing like bird­song.</p>
<p>Pla­to’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek tech­nol­o­gy explained in <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F20zQmyZa20">the new video above from<em> Lost in Time</em></a><em>,</em> a YouTube chan­nel whose <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2025/09/the-advanced-technology-of-ancient-rome.html">look at ancient Roman tech­nol­o­gy</a> we post­ed here on Open Cul­ture last year.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Most of the oth­ers were invent­ed for less gen­tle pur­pos­es: we have a nasty-look­ing flamethrow­er on wheels meant to breach stone fortress­es; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapid­ly than any bow­man; a nine-sto­ry-tall pro­to-tank ful­ly stocked with cat­a­pults and sol­diers ready to swarm a city; and a gigan­tic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and over­turn invad­ing war­ships. Yet as for­mi­da­ble as they sound, evi­dence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they func­tioned in actu­al bat­tle — remains scarce.</p>
<p>Much clear­er are records of the <em>Diolkos</em>, recent­ly men­tioned here when we fea­tured <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2026/10/the-megaprojects-even-the-ancient-romans-couldnt-pull-off.html">the megapro­jects that even ancient Rome could­n’t pull off</a>. Among those endeav­ors was a canal across the Isth­mus of Corinth, which would save ships hav­ing to take the long way around the Pelo­pon­nesian penin­su­la. Or rather, it would save them hav­ing to be dragged by a cou­ple hun­dred slaves over the <em>Diolkos</em>, a paved track­way built in the sixth cen­tu­ry BC. Using ramps and winch­es, ships could be shift­ed onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, mak­ing the whole sys­tem a pre­cur­sor of the rail­road, or per­haps an invert­ed ances­tor of the fer­ry still used to trans­port rail­way cars <a href="https://www.openculture.com/2025/03/why-there-isnt-a-bridge-from-italy-to-sicily.html">across the Strait of Messi­na</a>. Like the Romans, the Greeks also con­sid­ered dig­ging a canal, but to do so might have vio­lat­ed the inten­tions of Zeus, a bet­ter excuse not to build infra­struc­ture than some of those we hear in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry.</p>
<p><strong>Relat­ed Con­tent:</strong></p>
<p><a href="https://www.openculture.com/2026/02/an-animated-introduction-to-the-antikythera-mechanism.html">An Ani­mat­ed Intro­duc­tion to the Antikythera Mech­a­nism: The World’s First Ana­log Com­put­er from Ancient Greece</a></p>
<p><a href="https://www.openculture.com/2026/09/the-ancient-greek-water-clock-that-kept-the-most-accurate-time-for-1800-years.html">The Ancient Greek Water Clock That Kept the Most Accu­rate Time for 1,800 Years</a></p>

			<div id="post-1129000" class="post-1129000 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-animation-2 category-music">
      			<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/aFfW0DCoGBg?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>Ah, yes, “Auto­bahn.” From the moment the door slams and the igni­tion starts, prog rock­ers and pre-new wavers know a jour­ney is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band mem­bers still looked like well-mean­ing, book­ish hip­pies, 1974’s “Auto­bahn” is con­sid­ered Year Zero for the denizens of the Elec­tric Café, the four Ger­man robots who made human music with machines.</p>
<p>This cel-drawn ani­ma­tion by Roger Main­wood was made in 1979 to pro­mote “Auto­bahn,” after most of the cul­ture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bop­ping around pop cul­ture again. By that last year of the ’70s, <em>Omni</em> mag­a­zine was a year old, music was sift­ing through the shock­waves left by Bowie’s <em>Low</em> and <em>Heroes</em>, ana­log was flirt­ing with dig­i­tal, and the world was ready to dri­ve on that long, elec­tric high­way.</p>
<div class="oc-center-da">
<div data-fuse="22871471544"></div>
</div>

<p>Mainwood’s pro­tag­o­nist is part alien, part human, and he begins look­ing around in awe in his hip gog­gles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muy­bridge loop, only to wind up float­ing, fly­ing, sail­ing and swim­ming through a land­scape indebt­ed to Peter Max, Push Pin Stu­dios, under­ground comix, and 1930s mod­ernism.</p>
<p>Main­wood had just grad­u­at­ed from London’s Roy­al Col­lege of Art Film and Tele­vi­sion School, and was com­mis­sioned by John Halas, the Hun­gar­i­an immi­grant who became known as the Father of British Ani­ma­tion, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label want­ed to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cKkgdKXgntU">direct­ed a very UPA-influ­enced short called “Auto­ma­nia” in 1963</a>). Accord­ing to Main­wood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.</p>
<div class="oc-video-wrapper">
<div class="oc-video-container">
	<span class="youtube"><iframe loading="lazy" title="YouTube video player" class="youtube-player" type="text/html" width="640" height="505" src="//www.youtube.com/embed/wlVLd4bE7Ss?wmode=transparent&fs=1&hl=en&showsearch=0&rel=0&theme=dark" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe></span>
	</div>
<p>	<!-- /oc-video-embed -->
</p></div>
<p><!-- /oc-video-wrapper --></p>
<p>Main­wood avoid­ed any direct rep­re­sen­ta­tion of dri­ving or auto­mo­biles, much to his cred­it, which may be why the film holds its fas­ci­na­tion. The ani­ma­tor con­tin­ued in his field, wind­ing up a pro­duc­er of sev­er­al clas­sics of British ani­ma­tion, includ­ing <em>The Snow­man</em> and the chill­ing <em>When the Wind Blows</em>. As for the mean­ing of “Auto­bahn,” we’ll let Main­wood have the last word:</p>
<blockquote><p>Think­ing back to my thought process­es at that time, I remem­ber want­i­ng to specif­i­cal­ly not have con­ven­tion­al cars in the film. I want­ed a sense of a repet­i­tive jour­ney, and alien­ation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the soli­tary futur­is­tic fig­ure, pro­tect­ed by large gog­gles, mov­ing through and try­ing to con­nect with the jour­ney he is tak­ing. The auto­mo­bile “mon­sters” are delib­er­ate­ly threat­en­ing (I have nev­er been a big fan of cars or motor­ways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human con­tact (with dif­fer­ent coloured clones of him­self) he can nev­er do it. In the end he realis­es he is mak­ing the repet­i­tive and cir­cu­lar jour­ney alone but strides for­ward pur­pose­ful­ly at the end as he did in the begin­ning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!</p></blockquote>
<p>You can read more of <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20141222213552/http://kraftwerkonline.pagesperso-orange.fr/autobahncartoon2.html">an inter­view with </a>Main­wood<a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20141222213552/http://kraftwerkonline.pagesperso-orange.fr/autobahncartoon2.html"> here.</a></p>
<p>Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.</p>
